sentences.text: Last time we found the top of the hill: the one setting where every meter that can level is level.
But we found it by being told where it was.
A computer has no such luck. It cannot solve for the top with algebra, because every expected count passes through the S-curve.
All it can do, from wherever it stands, is feel the ground: which way is up, and how the slope is changing.
So how do you climb a hill you can only feel one spot at a time?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: climbing the hill.
Start small, with one slider. Hold the dial at its fitted place, 2.02, and stand Dune's slider in the wrong spot: on Cedar's level, minus 1.52.
Here is Dune's own hill: its height for every position of its slider.
From where we stand, we can't see it. We know just two things: the slope under our feet, and how fast that slope is changing.
That is enough to draw a parabola that matches the hill right here.
So jump to the top of the parabola: 0.96 to the right, to minus 0.56.
Do it again from the new spot. The second jump is tiny: 0.017 back to the left.
And we are there: minus 0.58. Two steps.
Where did 0.96 come from? Read it off the meter.
The tilt, we know: observed 7, expected 4.8, a gap of 2.2.
The second number is how readily the expected count moves when the slider does. Call it the wobble.
A patient near 50% adds the most to it. A patient near 0 or near 100% hardly adds at all.
For Dune's twelve patients, it comes to 2.29.
So the step is tilt over wobble: 2.2 divided by 2.29.
A gap of 2.2 to close, at 2.29 per unit of slider: move 0.96.
That division is what makes this more than walking uphill. It does not just say which way. It says how far.
Now the whole machine, from the plain guess. Every clinic can take its step at the same moment, because each step uses only that clinic's own patients.
Then the dial takes one step, with the sliders frozen.
But that unsettles every clinic, so the sliders step again. Then the dial. Then the sliders.
Watch the dial. After eight rounds it has only reached 1.91, on its way to 2.02.
Each round covers a fraction of what is left. Getting there takes 54 rounds.
And Elm steps down by about one unit every round, without end.
Here is why it is slow. This is the hill seen from above: the dial runs left to right, Birch's slider up and down.
The path is a staircase: up or down for the sliders, sideways for the dial.
And the ridge it is trying to follow runs diagonally. Turn the dial up, and every expected count rises, so every slider has to come down.
A staircase is a slow way along a diagonal.
How slow depends on something that should not matter: where we put zero.
Last episode, moving zero changed every gamma and no gap. It changes the climb too.
Record the risk factor five units higher, and the same alternation needs 3,125 rounds.
Put zero in the middle of the patients instead, and the ridge straightens: 21 rounds. That is what pprof_py does before it starts.
Let's gather it up.
A step is tilt over wobble. It says which way, and how far.
The sliders can all step at once. The dial steps in turn.
And taking turns climbs a diagonal ridge by staircase.
Every route here climbs toward the same top. They differ in how long they take.
So here is the obvious question. Could the sliders and the dial step together, straight along the ridge?
They can, and then it takes five steps. Next time: the arrow matrix.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
